Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.
slides: Welcome back. Sometimes every person in a question has two traits. For example, a student is in the upper grades or the lower grades. And the student walks to school, or doesn't.

slides.say: These are really our four regions again. A student can be upper and walk, or upper and not walk. Or the student can be lower and walk, or lower and not walk. Here a table is clearer than circles.

slides: Each row is one group, and each column is the other trait. And we add a total for every row and every column.

slides.say: Here's the trap in these questions. Say twenty percent of the women wear glasses, and thirty percent of the men wear glasses. What percent of everyone wears glasses?
at: Say twenty percent of the women

slides.say: A lot of students add, and say fifty percent. Others take the average, twenty-five percent. But twenty-five isn't guaranteed either. We don't know the group sizes yet.

slides: Why? Because the twenty percent is of the women, and the thirty percent is of the men. These are percents of different wholes.

slides.say: Let's see it in numbers. Put women and men in rows. Say there are forty women and sixty men, a hundred people. In the glasses column, twenty percent of forty is eight. Thirty percent of sixty is eighteen.
at: Put women and men in rows

slides.say: Eight plus eighteen is twenty-six. So twenty-six people out of a hundred wear glasses, twenty-six percent. Not fifty, and not twenty-five.
at: twenty-six people out of a hundred

slides.say: So find how many wear glasses in each group first. Add those counts, and compare with the total number of people. The table keeps the groups clear.
Now a club has eighty adults and twenty children. Twenty-five members take art, and thirty take language. At most how many adults take neither?

slides: We want as many adults outside the classes as possible. So we need as few adults in the classes as possible.

slides.say: Let the children take the class places first. All twenty children can take both classes. That leaves twenty-five minus twenty, five art places for adults. Thirty minus twenty leaves ten language places for adults.
Those ten language places need ten different adults. Can the five art students be among them? Yes. Then only ten adults take a class.
at: Then only ten adults take a class

slides.say: So eighty minus ten, seventy adults take neither. Our arrangement works. And we cannot have more, because at least ten adults must take language.

slides: The trap is answering about all members. Here the requested group is adults. Keep children and adults separate.

slides.say: One more application. There are twenty-four cars. Fourteen have air conditioning. Sixteen carry three people each. Every other car carries one person. At least how many people are in air-conditioned cars?

slides: The groups count cars, not people. We want as few people as possible in the air-conditioned cars. So first minimize the overlap with three-person cars.

slides.say: Fourteen plus sixteen is thirty. Thirty minus twenty-four is six. So at least six air-conditioned cars carry three people.
The other fourteen minus six, eight air-conditioned cars carry one person. Six times three is eighteen people. Eight times one is eight people. Eighteen plus eight is twenty-six people.

Why is this the minimum? Replacing a one-person car with a three-person car adds two people. We used the smallest possible overlap, so we used the fewest people. Check what each group counts before using the answer. Now try the guided question. I'll see you in the next video.
